description: Team One Humanity presents ONEIROS, an innovative astronaut health-support system designed for long-duration space missions. By combining emerging technologies with human-centered design, ONEIROS aims to move beyond traditional health monitoring and explore new ways to understand, support, and protect astronaut health and performance as humans venture farther into space.
summary:
Long-duration space missions present a medical challenge: astronauts must recognize changes in their own health while operating far from Earth, where medical resources are limited and communication with flight surgeons may be delayed.

Our team developed ONEIROS, a space medicine software prototype that brings physiological assessments, biomedical sensing, computer vision, and AI-assisted analysis into one platform. We are exploring how these tools can help astronauts monitor changes in cardiovascular function and physical performance by comparing measurements against their individual baselines.

ONEIROS also uses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to connect assessment findings with relevant space medicine research. We are developing structured reports that summarize physiological trends and potential concerns for flight surgeons to review during medical consultations, while helping astronauts better understand their health.

We are also exploring future integration with existing medical technologies aboard the International Space Station.

The prototype remains under development, with ongoing work focused on system integration and measurement reliability. Our goal is to support astronaut self-assessment and medical follow-up during future exploration missions. Beyond spaceflight, this approach could also be adapted to support patient monitoring and clinical review in hospitals on Earth.
details:
"We cannot prevent every challenge the human body faces in space, but we can work to recognize the changes before they become greater risks"

- Team One Humanity -

1. From Physiological Measurements to Health Insights

ONEIROS was developed to investigate how astronauts can assess changes in their health during long-duration space missions, particularly when immediate medical support from Earth may not be available.

Our approach combines physiological assessments, biomedical sensing, machine learning, and research-based AI within a single software environment. The system is being developed as a research prototype to support astronaut self-assessment and flight surgeon review, rather than provide independent medical diagnoses.

The central idea is to turn individual measurements into information that can be tracked, interpreted, and reviewed over time.

2. Physiological Assessment and Data Collection

Our computer vision assessments were developed by examining established physiological measurement methods and published research relevant to human performance, fatigue, and cardiovascular monitoring. Medical perspectives also informed our selection of measurements, with attention to their physiological relevance, practical limitations, and suitability for repeated assessments.

Rather than inventing new medical tests, we are investigating how existing measurement principles can be adapted into accessible, camera-based tools.

Our assessment modules include:

Eye Blink Duration Test: Drawing on research into ocular behavior, alertness, and fatigue, this assessment uses facial landmark tracking to measure blink frequency and duration. We are investigating whether changes in these characteristics may provide useful indicators for fatigue-related research.

This test was based on the "Real-Time Drowsiness Detection to Improve Driver Safety."

(https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0001457517304372?via%3Dihub)

Arm Raised Test: Based on motion-tracking and human movement assessment principles, this test uses body landmark detection to measure arm movements and repetitions. It allows us to explore changes in motor performance and movement consistency, which may be relevant to understanding physical performance during spaceflight.

This test was based on the gold standard fatigue detection test from "NASA Psychomotor Vigilance Task." (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0001457517304372?via%3Dihub)

Heart Rate Assessment: This assessment applies remote photoplethysmography (rPPG), an established optical technique that estimates pulse-related signals through subtle changes in facial skin color. We are evaluating its potential for non-contact cardiovascular monitoring.

Each assessment produces numerical measurements that can be organized by participant, assessment type, and session. Repeated measurements allow us to compare results against individual baselines and investigate changes over time.

Our development is informed by published physiological and space medicine research, alongside medical input within our interdisciplinary team. We consider the scientific rationale behind each measurement, the conditions required for reliable data collection, and the limitations of applying these methods to astronaut health research.

Based on: "GRGB rPPG: An Efficient Low-Complexity Remote Photoplethysmography-Based Algorithm for Heart Rate Estimation." (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9952130/)

3. How Machine Learning and AI Work Together

One of the main objectives of ONEIROS is to connect physiological measurements with analytical tools that help users understand their significance.

The proposed workflow begins when an astronaut completes an assessment. Computer vision algorithms extract measurable features, which are then organized into structured data and passed to the analysis layer.

Machine Learning — Identifying Patterns

The machine learning component is being developed to analyze physiological features across repeated assessments.

Rather than evaluating each measurement independently, the model can investigate relationships between multiple indicators, changes from personal baselines, and trends across sessions.

For example, changes in blink duration, movement performance, and estimated heart rate may provide a more informative picture when examined together than when viewed as separate results.

Our research focuses on determining whether these patterns can help identify unusual changes that warrant additional assessment. Model performance, sensitivity, and false alerts require evaluation using appropriate datasets.

RAG-Based AI — Explaining the Findings

Machine learning and the AI assistant serve different purposes.

The ML component examines numerical patterns, while the retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system is designed to explain findings using relevant space medicine literature.

When assessment results and analytical findings are made available to the AI assistant, it can retrieve related research, provide physiological context, and help users understand possible explanations and measurement limitations.

For instance, if an assessment shows a change in cardiovascular indicators, the assistant can connect the observation with research on cardiovascular adaptation to microgravity without treating the result as a confirmed medical condition.

This creates a connection between measurement, pattern analysis, and scientific interpretation, rather than presenting AI-generated explanations without supporting evidence.

4. Biomedical Sensor Lab and Spaceflight Simulation

Computer vision is only one part of the ONEIROS research environment.

Our Sensor Lab explores additional biomedical measurements, including cardiovascular signals and other physiological indicators relevant to human spaceflight.

The simulation component allows users to examine how physiological responses may differ under selected spaceflight-related conditions.

For example, users can explore cardiovascular and fluid-distribution changes associated with altered gravity and learn which measurements may be useful for studying those responses.

These simulations provide an educational and research environment for understanding physiological mechanisms. They are clearly distinguished from actual sensor recordings.

The broader engineering objective is to support future integration of compatible biomedical instruments and existing spaceflight medical technologies, including equipment used aboard the International Space Station.

5. Medical Reporting and Flight Surgeon Workflow

Collecting measurements is only useful if the information can be reviewed and acted upon appropriately.

ONEIROS is being designed to organize assessment results into structured reports that flight surgeons and medical teams could use during routine medical consultations.

A report would bring together:

  • Recorded physiological measurements and assessment dates.
  • Comparisons with individual baseline values.
  • Changes observed across multiple sessions.
  • ML-identified patterns, where supported by validated models.
  • Research references and explanatory context.
  • Measurement limitations and observations requiring follow-up.

This reporting approach would allow medical teams to examine an astronaut's physiological history before a consultation, rather than relying on isolated measurements or verbal descriptions alone.

It could also help astronauts recognize changes worth discussing with their flight surgeon, particularly during missions where communication opportunities are limited.

6. Software Architecture and Development Tools

Our development approach emphasizes modularity so that individual assessment tools, sensors, and analytical components can be developed and tested independently.

Computer Vision: Python, OpenCV, and MediaPipe are used for camera-based landmark detection, movement tracking, and physiological feature extraction.

Backend Integration: FastAPI-based REST interfaces provide a framework for connecting assessment applications with the central platform. Structured JSON data supports the exchange of measurements and assessment results.

Machine Learning: Python-based analytical workflows are being developed to investigate individual baseline deviations, multivariable physiological patterns, and anomaly detection.

AI and Knowledge Retrieval: RAG connects language-model explanations with selected space medicine research and technical references, including NASA human health and performance resources.

User Interface: The web platform provides access to assessments, sensor simulations, research information, session records, and reporting functions.

Separating these components also makes it possible to evaluate individual methods before incorporating them into a larger analytical workflow.

7. Engineering and Medical Research Considerations

Several factors have influenced our development decisions.

Camera-based assessments offer accessibility, but their measurements can be affected by lighting, motion, camera quality, and participant positioning. These limitations are particularly relevant to remote heart rate estimation.

Physiological variability presents another challenge. We are investigating repeated baseline measurements and within-person comparisons to better understand how normal variation differs from potentially meaningful changes.

For machine learning, our priorities include data quality, appropriate training and evaluation datasets, explainability, and controlling false alerts.

For AI-assisted interpretation, source reliability and clear distinctions between measured observations, model-generated findings, and scientific explanations are essential.

We are also considering medical data privacy, interoperability, and the operational constraints of future exploration missions.

8. Intended Impact and Future Development

ONEIROS is still under active development. Our current work focuses on connecting assessment modules, improving data collection, developing analytical methods, and evaluating measurement reliability.

A longer-term objective is to investigate interoperability with existing spaceflight medical systems, allowing future versions to incorporate additional physiological data sources.

We believe the project's potential value lies in connecting three groups that depend on the same information: astronauts performing self-assessments, engineers developing reliable measurement systems, and flight surgeons reviewing physiological changes.

As exploration missions move farther from Earth, this approach could contribute to more informed onboard health assessments and better preparation for medical consultations.

The underlying methods may also have applications in hospitals and remote healthcare environments on Earth, where repeated physiological measurements and structured clinical reporting can support medical review.
